liturgical_day: Memorial of Saint Peter Claver, Priest
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: The kingdom is yours
theme: Christ blesses those who prefer his kingdom to passing security and warns those already satisfied with the world's consolation.
introduction: Jesus lifts his eyes toward the disciples and announces a reversal that only God's kingdom can make intelligible. Poverty, hunger, tears, and rejection are not good in themselves. The Fathers insist that the blessing belongs to those who freely prefer Christ to riches, hunger for righteousness, mourn sin, and endure contempt because they bear the Son of Man's name. Luke also preserves four corresponding woes. Christ does not condemn possessions as though material things were evil; he condemns the heart that treats entrusted goods as private consolation and refuses their common purpose. Nor does he forbid every smile or good reputation. He exposes self-satisfaction, pleasure without repentance, and praise purchased by abandoning truth. The poor may still covet, and the rich may practice generous stewardship. The decisive question is where the heart seeks its good. Jesus places present appearances under eternity's judgment: want borne with faith will not have the last word, while comfort closed against God and neighbor has already spent its reward.
hero_alt: Jesus lifts his eyes toward his disciples and proclaims the blessings and woes on the plain in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and luminous geometry
closing: The blessings and woes ask not only what we possess but what possesses us. Poverty can remain covetous, while wealth can become grateful service. Christ looks beneath each condition to the direction of desire. Do we prefer his command to possessions? Do we hunger for righteousness? Do we grieve over sin and suffering, trusting him for joy? Will we remain faithful when his name costs approval? Consolation chosen instead of God ends with this life. Fullness that never notices Lazarus creates its own famine. Laughter that will not mourn evil becomes incapable of heavenly joy, and universal praise may mean truth has been traded for flattery. Yet the promises are stronger than the threats. The kingdom already belongs to Christ's poor; future fullness answers present hunger; pure joy awaits repentant tears; and the Lord himself measures the reward of those rejected for him. Ask for freedom to use every gift as stewardship and to value God's judgment above applause. The reversal begins wherever the heart releases passing consolation to receive Christ as its lasting good.

verses.text: And he, lifting up his eyes upon his disciples, said: Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verses.author: St Basil the Great
verses.insight: Basil distinguishes chosen evangelical poverty from mere lack. Blessedness belongs to the disciple who freely prefers Christ's command to worldly riches.
verses.commentary: Basil warns that material poverty by itself does not make a person blessed. Someone may own little and still be ruled by covetous desire. The blessing concerns a free allegiance: the disciple values Christ's command above wealth and follows the Lord who accepted poverty for our sake. This freedom makes room for the kingdom because possessions are no longer the heart's final security. Jesus blesses the poverty shaped by discipleship, in which earthly goods cease to rival the good promised and embodied by Christ.
verses.source_label: St Basil the Great, Homily on Psalm 33, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:20–23

verses.text: Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verses.author: St Gregory of Nyssa
verses.insight: Gregory directs hunger toward righteousness, the soul's true food. Unlike passing pleasures, virtue opens into a joy that does not fail.
verses.commentary: Gregory compares the body's appetites with the desires of the soul. Some feed upon reputation and passing pleasure, but the blessed hunger is for what is good in itself: the fullness of righteousness. Created enjoyments cannot finally satisfy anyone who makes them an ultimate end. The pursuit of virtue, however, receives the very good it desires and leads to unfailing joy. Jesus joins hunger and tears to fulfillment and laughter. The present ache of a soul longing for holiness is not purposeless emptiness; God will answer it with his joy.
verses.source_label: St Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 4 on the Beatitudes, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:20–23

verses.text: Blessed shall you be when men hate you, when they separate you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil for the Son of Man's sake.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede locates the blessing in rejection suffered specifically for Christ. Human exclusion cannot sever a disciple from the Lord who finds and strengthens his own.
verses.commentary: Bede does not call every form of unpopularity blessed. The decisive phrase is “for the Son of Man's sake.” A disciple may be expelled, reproached, and have the Christian name treated as evil, yet those judgments cannot injure the heart loved by Christ. When earthly communities cast the faithful person out, Christ finds and strengthens that person; when the Crucified's name is mocked, he raises those united to him. The blessing rests not in quarrelsomeness, but in steadfast communion with Jesus when fidelity brings undeserved rejection.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:20–23

verses.text: Be glad in that day and rejoice, for behold, your reward is great in heaven. For their fathers did the same things to the prophets.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Chrysostom measures the promised reward by the dignity of the one who promises it. Christ's “great” names a gift beyond human estimation.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom asks who speaks the promise. If a human teacher called a reward great, the word would remain limited by that person's judgment and resources. Here the Lord speaks, and eternal treasures are in his hands. His declaration assures persecuted disciples of a reward surpassing human conception. Their suffering places them beside the prophets, who endured hostility because they spoke God's truth. Rejoicing does not deny persecution's pain. It interprets that pain by Christ's trustworthy judgment: rejection for his sake cannot cancel the heavenly good he pledges.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:20–23

verses.text: But woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Ambrose says wealth itself is not condemned; fault lies in the possessive heart. Gifts entrusted for the common good become perilous when hoarded.
verses.commentary: Ambrose distinguishes riches from their misuse. Wealth presents temptations, but it can also become an occasion for virtue. Christ's warning falls upon the person who receives abundance without gratitude and hides from others what was entrusted for the common good. The rich bear greater responsibility because more has been received. Present consolation becomes dangerous when accumulation itself supplies the heart's pleasure and replaces eternal hope. Money is not the culprit; the possessor's closed desire is. Goods serve salvation when received thankfully and shared, not when guarded as the soul's reward.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:24–26

verses.text: Woe to you who are filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall mourn and weep.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede contrasts satisfaction in one's own desires with hunger for true goodness. The woe exposes a fullness that leaves no appetite for righteousness.
verses.commentary: Bede reads the warning through its opposite blessing. Those who hunger for works of righteousness are happy because their desire reaches toward the true good. Those pleased with their own desires and feeling no such hunger are spiritually endangered, however satisfied they appear. He recalls the rich man who feasted while ignoring Lazarus, only to discover unbearable hunger after death. Christ does not condemn nourishment or every cheerful countenance. He unmasks self-sufficiency: a life filled with private pleasure but empty of mercy and repentance will finally experience the lack it refused to recognize.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:24–26

verses.text: Woe to you when men bless you, for their fathers did the same things to the false prophets.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Chrysostom distinguishes good witness from vainglory. The disciple seeks God's glory but refuses to make popular approval the judge of truth.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom explains that this woe does not contradict Christ's command to let good works shine. The purpose of visible goodness is God's glory, not self-exaltation. Vainglory becomes destructive because it makes public opinion the standard of virtue and gives birth to further sins. Human praise passes quickly into oblivion and can be purchased by telling people what they wish to hear, as false prophets did. The remedy is to raise the heart toward God and accept his judgment. Approval may accompany fidelity, but it must never become the reward for which fidelity is exchanged.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homily 6 on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 6:24–26
